abstract: In this paper we present a quantum algorithm solving the triangle finding problem in unweighted graphs with query complexity $\tilde{O}(n^{5/4})$, where $n$ denotes the number of vertices in the graph. This improves the previous upper bound $O(n^{9/7})=O(n^{1.285...})$ recently obtained by Lee, Magniez and Santha. Our result shows, for the first time, that in the quantum query complexity setting unweighted triangle finding is easier than its edge-weighted version, since for finding an edge-weighted triangle Belovs and Rosmanis proved that any quantum algorithm requires $\Omega(n^{9/7}/\sqrt{\log n})$ queries. Our result also illustrates some limitations of the non-adaptive learning graph approach used to obtain the previous $O(n^{9/7})$ upper bound since, even over unweighted graphs, any quantum algorithm for triangle finding obtained using this approach requires $\Omega(n^{9/7}/\sqrt{\log n})$ queries as well. To bypass the obstacles characterized by these lower bounds, our quantum algorithm uses combinatorial ideas exploiting the graph-theoretic properties of triangle finding, which cannot be used when considering edge-weighted graphs or the non-adaptive learning graph approach.

specification.problem: Triangle finding in an unweighted, undirected n-vertex graph G=(V,E) accessed through an adjacency-matrix query oracle: decide whether there exist three distinct vertices u,v,w with {u,v},{v,w},{u,w} all in E (and output such a triple if it exists). The abstract claims a quantum algorithm with query complexity \tilde{O}(n^{5/4}), improving the O(n^{9/7}) learning-graph bound of Lee, Magniez and Santha, and separating unweighted from edge-weighted triangle finding (for which an \Omega(n^{9/7}/\sqrt{\log n}) lower bound is known).
specification.reconstruction_scope: The abstract states only the problem, the query model implicitly, and the complexity bounds; it does not describe the algorithm's construction (its combinatorial decomposition, use of random vertex subsets, sparsification, or nested quantum-walk subroutines). Therefore the scoped reconstruction is: (i) a precise statement of the query model, the triangle predicate, and the claimed/comparison bounds; and (ii) ONE smallest useful concrete construction, chosen as an assumption: a textbook Grover search over vertex triples on a tiny explicit instance (n=4, vertices {0,1,2,3}, edges {01,02,12,23}, exactly one triangle {0,1,2}), which uses O(n^{3/2}) queries and is NOT the paper's \tilde{O}(n^{5/4}) algorithm. Outside scope: the paper's actual combinatorial algorithm, its analysis achieving n^{5/4}, the learning-graph lower bound argument, and the edge-weighted lower bound of Belovs and Rosmanis.

equations.label: Adjacency-matrix query oracle
equations.description: Standard quantum query oracle for graph problems in the adjacency-matrix model; one application counts as one query. Query complexity in the abstract is counted with respect to such an oracle.
equations.justification: Triangle finding query complexity results of this line of work (including the cited O(n^{9/7}) bound) are stated in the adjacency-matrix query model; the abstract mentions query complexity but does not define the oracle, so this is recalled background.
assumptions: Adjacency-matrix (edge-query) model rather than adjacency-list model.

equations.label: Triangle predicate
equations.latex: f(u,v,w) = A[u,v]\wedge A[v,w]\wedge A[u,w],\qquad u,v,w\in V \text{ pairwise distinct}
equations.description: Exact Boolean definition of when a triple of vertices forms a triangle; the triangle finding problem asks whether some triple has f=1 (and to output it). Evaluating f on one triple costs exactly 3 queries to O_G.
equations.abstract_quote: solving the triangle finding problem in unweighted graphs
equations.justification: Inferred from the problem name: a triangle in an unweighted graph is a 3-clique; the abstract does not spell out the predicate.
assumptions: Simple undirected graph (symmetric A, no self-loops).

equations.label: Claimed upper bound and comparison bounds
equations.description: The abstract's main claim (first relation), the fact that it improves the previous O(n^{9/7}) bound (second relation, since 5/4=1.25<9/7\approx1.2857), and the quoted lower bound for the edge-weighted variant and for non-adaptive learning-graph algorithms (third relation). These are asymptotic statements, not exact equalities.
equations.abstract_quote: query complexity $\tilde{O}(n^{5/4})$, where $n$ denotes the number of vertices in the graph. This improves the previous upper bound $O(n^{9/7})=O(n^{1.285...})$
equations.justification: Directly stated in the abstract; the weighted lower bound is quoted from the abstract's attribution to Belovs and Rosmanis.
assumptions: Bounded-error (e.g. success probability at least 2/3) query complexity, as is standard.

equations.label: Baseline Grover search over triples (scoped construction, not the paper's algorithm)
equations.description: Phase-oracle Grover iterate over all unordered vertex triples. Each U_f costs 3 queries to O_G (compute the three edge bits via eq_1 into ancillas, AND them into a phase, uncompute). This is the smallest useful construction consistent with the problem; it is a textbook baseline chosen because the abstract gives no construction details of the n^{5/4} algorithm.
equations.justification: No experiment_scope was supplied, so one minimal construction is chosen and labelled as an assumption; it reproduces the problem semantics (eq_2) but not the paper's complexity.
assumptions: Grover search over triples is used purely as a baseline; the paper's combinatorial algorithm is different and not reconstructable from the abstract.

equations.label: Grover iteration count and baseline query cost
equations.description: Standard Grover analysis for the baseline: with M unknown one uses exponential guessing of M or amplitude estimation, still O(\sqrt{N}) iterations. For the tiny instance N=4, M=1: \theta=\pi/6, k=1 and the success probability is \sin^2(\pi/2)=1 exactly. The resulting O(n^{3/2}) is strictly worse than the abstract's \tilde{O}(n^{5/4}).
equations.justification: Standard Grover/amplitude-amplification facts; included to make the baseline construction executable and to make explicit the gap to the claimed bound.
assumptions: Floor in k is a rounding choice; success probability is exact only when (2k+1)\theta=\pi/2.

equations.label: Tiny explicit instance
equations.description: Concrete instance with exactly one triangle. The triple index t is stored in a 2-qubit register with big-endian binary encoding (|t\rangle=|t_1 t_0\rangle, t = 2t_1+t_0); the triple-to-vertices map is a fixed classical table used inside U_f.
equations.justification: Chosen as the smallest nontrivial instance (N=4, M=1) for which one Grover iteration succeeds with probability exactly 1.
assumptions: Instance and index encoding are arbitrary choices for the baseline.

registers.name: triple_index
registers.role: Holds the index t of a candidate vertex triple {u,v,w}; the search register of the baseline Grover construction (eq_4, eq_6).

registers.name: edge_bits
registers.role: Ancillas receiving A[u,v], A[v,w], A[u,w] via three applications of O_G (eq_1); uncomputed after use.

registers.name: phase_ancilla
registers.role: Prepared in |-\rangle so that writing f=A[u,v]\wedge A[v,w]\wedge A[u,w] into it implements the phase oracle U_f of eq_4.

specification.initial_state: |0\rangle^{\otimes 2}_{\text{triple\_index}}\otimes|000\rangle_{\text{edge\_bits}}\otimes|1\rangle_{\text{phase\_ancilla}}; after H^{\otimes 2} on triple_index and H on phase_ancilla this becomes |\psi_0\rangle\otimes|000\rangle\otimes|-\rangle with |\psi_0\rangle=\frac12\sum_{t=0}^{3}|t\rangle.

steps.description: Prepare the uniform superposition |\psi_0\rangle over the N=\binom{n}{3} triple indices (N=4 for the tiny instance) and the phase ancilla in |-\rangle.

Oracle step: controlled on the triple index, query O_G three times to load A[u,v], A[v,w], A[u,w] into edge_bits; apply a Toffoli-type AND of the three edge bits into the phase ancilla (giving phase (-1)^{f}); uncompute edge_bits with three further queries (or, counting as in eq_5, 3 queries per evaluation with uncomputation folded in). This realizes U_f.
Apply the diffusion operator 2|\psi_0\rangle\langle\psi_0|-I on triple_index, completing one Grover iterate \mathcal{G}.
Repeat the oracle and diffusion steps k times with k=\lfloor (\pi/4)\sqrt{N/M}\rfloor; for the tiny instance k=1. If M is unknown, use the standard exponentially-increasing-iteration schedule.

specification.measurement: Measure triple_index in the computational basis to obtain an index t; for the tiny instance the outcome is t=0 (triangle {0,1,2}) with probability exactly 1 after k=1 iteration.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Decode t into vertices {u,v,w} via the fixed triple table (eq_6) and verify with 3 classical queries that A[u,v]=A[v,w]=A[u,w]=1; output the triangle if verified, otherwise report 'no triangle' (repeat O(1) times to boost confidence when M is unknown).
assumptions: No experiment_scope was provided, so the smallest useful construction (Grover search over vertex triples on a 4-vertex instance) was chosen; this is explicitly a baseline, not a reconstruction of the paper's \tilde{O}(n^{5/4}) algorithm.
Adjacency-matrix query model with bounded-error success criterion.
Simple undirected unweighted graph; triple index register uses big-endian binary encoding with a fixed classical triple table.
All statements about the paper's algorithm beyond its complexity bound are unknown; nothing about random vertex subsets, sparsification, or nested quantum walks has been asserted as sourced.
missing_information: The actual structure of the \tilde{O}(n^{5/4}) algorithm: the combinatorial decomposition of the vertex set, the subroutines (e.g. which quantum walks or searches are nested), their parameters, and how the n^{5/4} exponent arises.
The precise 'graph-theoretic properties of triangle finding' exploited and why they fail for edge-weighted graphs and for non-adaptive learning graphs.
The hidden polylogarithmic factors in \tilde{O} and the success-probability guarantee.
Whether the algorithm outputs a triangle or only decides existence, and its time (as opposed to query) complexity.
The proof that non-adaptive learning-graph algorithms require \Omega(n^{9/7}/\sqrt{\log n}) queries even on unweighted graphs.
